title: We’ll See by Richard Nelson at The Public #wellsee #thepublictheater ...
transcript: One of the riskiest works on a New York stage right now depicts five people sitting around a table. The catch is that they're anticipating the results of the 2026 Midterm Election the night of November 3rd. When these four left-leaning adult siblings convene up in Rhinebeck, New York on this fateful night, they try their best to have a normal evening of food, drink, and pleasantries, having made a pact to not speak *his* name. Of course, they can't avoid their anxieties, and some politics do bleed into the conversation, but for the most part, it's a cozy night of catching up. These characters aren't especially remarkable, but they are fully realized and likely familiar in one way or another to New York theatre audiences, which tend to skew older and whiter. I found the piece to be a bit long for something without a strong narrative arc, and I personally didn't resonate with these characters all that much. Yet, the temporal immediacy of the piece combined with the strong, naturalistic performances gives it a slightly docu-esque quality, consistently dangling you between feeling immersed like a fly on the wall in their world and feeling startlingly aware that it's your world, too. I attended the show the night before the election, of which the results are still to be determined at the time of this recording. What makes the piece so excitingly ephemeral but risky, in my opinion, is that there's no way to tell how it'll land once all the chips fall. It could become a relieving retrospective, or sour like milk. If anyone sees it after the election, please report back.
classificationReason: Creator attended Richard Nelson's production at The Public and offers a clear first-hand opinion — noting the piece feels long, that they didn't personally connect with the characters, but praising the naturalistic performances and temporal immediacy.
